newsitem.title: USA: New England fishing regulators eye new restrictions.
newsitem.headline: New England fishing regulators eye new restrictions.

text.p: The New England Fishery Council Wednesday renewed the debate over how to protect groundfish stocks that scientists warn have been harvested to the point of collapse in the Gulf of Maine and Georges Bank.

A report prepared for the panel that regulates commercial fishing off the New England coast recommends fishing for valuable species of haddock, cod and yellowtail flounder be cut by 41 percent, and fishing for cod in the Gulf of Maine reduced 74 percent.

To achieve the limits, the report advised lowering the number of fishing days by 50 percent for vessels, which means 88 allowable days at sea for "fleet" vessels, and closing off additional areas of the Gulf of Maine to any fishing.

The weight of the new restrictions will fall heaviest on fishermen who rely on groundfish as their main source of income and use all of the "days at sea" allocated to them. Many of them already opted to sell their vessels to the government after the 1994 fishing crisis.

"This is a crisis situation here. I've never seen that many people at a meeting," said Rodney Avila, a New Bedford, Mass. fisherman, pointing to the dozens of fishermen packing the Council meeting in a Peabody hotel.

The report set targets for 1997 fishing season of 5,646 tonnes of Georges Bank cod, 6,108 tonnes of Georges Bank haddock, 1,206 tonnes of Georges Bank yellowtail flounder, 2,605 metric tonnes of Gulf of Maine cod and 824 metric tonnes of Southern New England yellowtail flounder.

Andrew Rosenberg, the New England administrator for the National Marines Fisheries Service, said the report indicates previous restrictions have stopped overfishing in some area, but the stocks have not yet replenished themselves.

"We said end overfishing all of the stocks and we have stopped overfishing. But we are not rebuilding fast enough," he said. "The report by no means says 'oh my God we have a big disaster on our hands.' Nobody is talking about putting an entire fleet sector out of business."
There U.S. government is expected to issue regulations for the fishing year that begins May 1 in late Janaury.
An industry consultant warned that the New England region may never recover its market share in fishing or rebuild collapsed infrastructure if the strictest of the proposed regulations were adopted.

"Icelandic, Norwegian, Russian, they all come in to grab the market share," said Robert J. Learson of R.J. Learson Associates of Hamilton, Mass. "When all of a sudden the fish come back, you've lost your market share. How do you get it back?"
